name: Bideford, Devon
hover_description: Bideford, 1682: Site of the last judicial witch executions in England. Temperance Lloyd, Susanna Edwards, and Mary Trembles hanged at Exeter; tried on Bideford evidence.
panel_description:
Bideford, a small port town in north Devon, is the site of the last judicial witch executions in England: Temperance Lloyd, Susanna Edwards, and Mary Trembles were hanged at Exeter on 25 August 1682, tried on indictments arising from examinations conducted in the Bideford borough court. The three women were elderly, poor, and locally feared — Lloyd had been under community suspicion for approximately thirty years before her 1682 prosecution. Their executions occurred at a moment when elite judicial skepticism about witchcraft was already pronounced in England, making Bideford a late provincial outlier rather than a product of any systematic institutional campaign.

  Gaskill's research situates the Bideford executions within the gap between popular and elite belief that characterized the final decades of English witch prosecution: the accused women were genuinely feared in their community, but several educated contemporaries expressed skepticism about the evidence. The case was constructed through the normal machinery of the English borough examination and assize system — no special commission, no Matthew Hopkins-style witch-finder — which makes the executions a product of ordinary community accusation dynamics rather than extraordinary prosecutorial pressure.

  The Bideford confessions, obtained through borough examination without formal torture, illustrate the examination-shaped testimony dynamic Ginzburg identifies: the accused women's statements about their diabolical involvement were structured by the categories supplied by their examiners. The familiar-spirit tradition persists in the Bideford confessions, consistent with the late seventeenth-century continuity of the English familiar-spirit framework documented by Wilby. A public memorial was erected in Bideford in 2008 commemorating the three women as the last judicial victims of English witch prosecution.
administrative_context: Bideford was a small port town in north Devon, and the last English witch executions arose from accusations and examinations conducted there. The three women tried were poor, elderly, and local to Bideford; they were tried at the Exeter Summer Assizes in 1682 on indictments from the Bideford borough court. Devon had seen relatively few witch prosecutions compared to Essex and the eastern counties, making the Bideford case a late provincial outlier rather than part of a sustained regional pattern.
witchcraft_trials_significance:
The Bideford executions of August 1682 are the last judicial witch executions in England — three poor elderly women, Temperance Lloyd, Susanna Edwards, and Mary Trembles, hanged at Exeter on charges of maleficium and diabolical compact. The trials occurred at a moment when elite judicial skepticism about witchcraft prosecution was increasing in England: they predated the formal repeal of the Witchcraft Act by only fifty-four years (1736), and the case was already controversial among educated contemporaries.

  Gaskill's historical analysis notes that the Bideford case illustrates the gap between popular belief (the accused were genuinely feared in their community) and judicial opinion (several prominent observers expressed skepticism about the evidence). The case is also notable for the direct participation of the borough recorder and local magistrates in constructing the accusations, suggesting that the 1682 prosecutions reflected local community dynamics — neighbors with longstanding grievances against the accused — rather than any panic or institutional pressure from above.

key_magistrates.name: Thomas Gist
key_magistrates.contribution_to_trials: Presided over the borough examinations; conducted initial interrogations; forwarded the case to the Exeter Assizes

persecution_timeline.1682: Temperance Lloyd examined in July; confessions extracted from all three women; tried at Exeter Summer Assizes; Temperance Lloyd, Susanna Edwards, and Mary Trembles hanged 25 August 1682

affected_population.geographic_extent: Bideford and surrounding north Devon community
affected_population.social_reach: Three elderly impoverished women; community with longstanding belief in their harmful practices

scholarly_analysis.clark_perspective: Clark's analysis of the later English prosecutions notes the Bideford case as evidence that popular belief in maleficium persisted robustly in English communities long after elite skepticism had made prosecution increasingly rare.
scholarly_analysis.hutton_perspective: Hutton identifies the Bideford women as fitting the classic English accused profile: elderly, poor, with reputations for magical harm built up over years of community tension — the demographic modal type identified by Macfarlane and Thomas in the Essex material.
scholarly_analysis.ginzburg_perspective: The Bideford confessions, obtained through borough examination without formal torture, illustrate the examination-shaped testimony dynamic Ginzburg identifies: the accused women's statements about their diabolical involvement were structured by the categories supplied by their examiners.

legacy_and_historiographical_importance: The Bideford executions mark the effective close of English witch prosecution under the 1563/1604 Witchcraft Acts. Malcolm Gaskill's research on the case provides the most detailed modern analysis. A public memorial was erected in Bideford in 2008 commemorating the three women.
primary_sources: Bideford Borough Court records; Exeter Assize records; contemporary pamphlet A True and Impartial Relation of the Informations Against Three Witches (1682)
source_method: Bideford Borough Records; Devon Record Office; analyzed in Gaskill, 'Witchcraft in Early Modern Kent,' in Sharpe and Golden (eds.), Witchcraft in Early Modern England (2003); Hutton, The Witch (2017); Levack, The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe (2006)
